title: Car Fleet
statement:
There is a single road leading to a finish line at position `target` (miles). `n` cars are on the road at distinct starting positions `position[i]` (all smaller than `target`), and car `i` drives toward the finish at a constant speed of `speed[i]` miles per hour.

A car can never pass another car. If a faster car catches up to a slower car ahead of it, it has to slow down and drive at the speed of the slower car, and from then on they travel together as one **fleet**. A car that catches up exactly at the finish line also counts as joining that fleet. A single car is also a fleet, and fleets never change after they form.

Count how many distinct fleets arrive at the finish line.

All times are exact rational numbers, so ties matter: two cars (or fleets) that would arrive at exactly the same moment belong to the same fleet. Compare arrival times without floating-point arithmetic.
inputFormat:
The first line contains two integers `target` and `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains two integers `position[i]` and `speed[i]`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the number of fleets that reach the finish line.
constraints: 0 ≤ position[i] < target, all positions are distinct

examples.explanation: Arrival times alone are 10, 8, 10 and 8 hours. The car at 10 is slower than the car at 12 ahead of it, so it forms the second fleet. The car at 4 reaches the finish at time 8, but it is stuck behind the fleet at position 10 and arrives at 10 with it; likewise the car at 0 (10 hours) merges. Result: 2 fleets.
Each car behind is slower than the car in front of it (times 90, 40, 23.3 from the back), so nobody catches up and there are 3 fleets.

The car at 9 needs 2 hours, same as the car at 13, so they meet exactly at the finish and form one fleet. The car at 6 needs 4.5 hours and is slower, so it is a new fleet. The car at 0 would need about 2.1 hours, so it catches up with that fleet and merges into it.

hints: Sort the cars by starting position. A car can only ever be blocked by the car directly in front of it.
For each car compute the time it would take alone: (target - position) / speed. Walk from the car nearest the finish to the farthest.
If a car's own time is greater than the time of the fleet ahead, it never catches up and starts a new fleet; otherwise it merges. Compare times with cross-multiplication to avoid floats.

             fmt(20, [(0, 2), (4, 2), (10, 1), (12, 1)]), fmt(100, [(10, 1), (20, 2), (30, 3)]),

             fmt(10, [(0, 10), (5, 5)]), fmt(7, [(0, 3), (1, 6), (2, 9)]),
             fmt(1000000, [(0, 1), (999999, 1)])]
    for _ in range(70):
        T = rng.randint(2, 30)
